# Sacubitril/Valsartan in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of morbidity, mortality, and hospitalization worldwide, affecting an estimated 64 million people [1]. Despite advances in neurohormonal blockade with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, residual risk remains high [2]. Sacubitril/valsartan, the first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), represents a major therapeutic advance, particularly in HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [3].

## Mechanism of Action

The natriuretic peptide system counteracts the deleterious effects of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) by promoting natriuresis, vasodilation, and inhibition of fibrosis and hypertrophy [4]. Neprilysin is a neutral endopeptidase that degrades natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [5]. Inhibiting neprilysin augments these beneficial peptides; however, neprilysin also degrades angiotensin II, so its inhibition alone could activate the RAAS [6]. Sacubitril/valsartan combines the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril (LBQ657 active metabolite) with the ARB valsartan, simultaneously enhancing natriuretic peptide signaling while blocking the angiotensin II type 1 receptor [7]. Earlier attempts combining neprilysin inhibition with ACE inhibition (omapatrilat) were abandoned due to unacceptable angioedema risk from dual bradykinin accumulation [8].

## Pivotal Clinical Trial Evidence

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial randomized 8,442 patients with NYHA class II–IV HFrEF to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril [9]. The trial was stopped early after sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20%, with a 16% reduction in all-cause mortality [9]. Benefits were consistent across subgroups and extended to symptom burden and quality of life [10]. Subsequent analyses demonstrated reductions in sudden cardiac death and improvements in measures of disease progression [11]. The PIONEER-HF trial extended this evidence to hospitalized patients with acute decompensated HFrEF, showing greater reductions in NT-proBNP compared with enalapril and a favorable safety profile when initiated in-hospital [12]. The TRANSITION study further supported safe in-hospital initiation across a range of clinical scenarios [13].

In HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), the PARAGON-HF trial narrowly missed its primary endpoint, with a rate ratio of 0.87 for total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death (p=0.06) [14]. Prespecified analyses suggested benefit in patients with ejection fraction below the normal range and in women [15]. These findings informed a broadened regulatory label in the United States for patients with "below normal" ejection fraction [16].

## Clinical Use and Practical Considerations

Guidelines now recommend ARNI as a cornerstone of HFrEF therapy, either replacing an ACE inhibitor/ARB or as initial therapy [17,18]. A washout period of at least 36 hours is required when switching from an ACE inhibitor to avoid angioedema [19]. Common adverse effects include hypotension, hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction, and, less commonly, angioedema [20]. Sacubitril/valsartan demonstrated renal protective signals relative to enalapril, with slower decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate [21]. NT-proBNP, rather than BNP, should be used for biomarker monitoring because neprilysin inhibition raises BNP levels [22].

Real-world registries have confirmed effectiveness and tolerability outside trial settings, though uptake and dose titration remain suboptimal [23]. The drug also produces favorable reverse remodeling, with reductions in left ventricular volumes and improvements in ejection fraction demonstrated in the PROVE-HF study [24]. Beneficial effects on functional capacity and atrial remodeling have also been reported [25].

## Cost-Effectiveness and Implementation

Cost-effectiveness analyses generally support sacubitril/valsartan as providing reasonable value relative to ACE inhibitors in HFrEF, though affordability concerns persist in many health systems [26]. Strategies to improve guideline-directed medical therapy implementation, including in-hospital initiation and simultaneous "four-pillar" therapy, are increasingly advocated [27].

## Emerging and Future Directions

The role of ARNI continues to expand. Studies have explored its use following acute myocardial infarction; the PARADISE-MI trial did not show a significant reduction in cardiovascular outcomes versus ramipril [28]. Interest persists in combining ARNI with sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors as part of comprehensive disease-modifying therapy [29]. Ongoing investigation addresses optimal sequencing, dosing in vulnerable populations, and effects across the full ejection fraction spectrum [30].

## Conclusion

Sacubitril/valsartan has transformed the management of HFrEF, offering mortality and morbidity benefits beyond conventional RAAS inhibition through its dual mechanism. While its role in HFpEF remains more nuanced, the totality of evidence supports earlier and broader adoption, with continued efforts needed to overcome barriers to implementation.
